items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "tephra".
items.answer: Fragments of volcanic material ejected into the air during an eruption, from fine ash to large volcanic bombs
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: fragments of volcanic material ejected into the air during an eruption, from fine ash to large volcanic bombs. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: An eruption of a volcano in Kamchatka ejected about 85.2 km³ of tephra. The VEI scale is logarithmic: VEI 2 ≥ 0.001 km³, VEI 3 ≥ 0.01, VEI 4 ≥ 0.1, VEI 5 ≥ 1, VEI 6 ≥ 10, VEI 7 ≥ 100 km³. Assign the eruption a VEI. How does its ejected volume compare with Eyjafjallajökull 2010 (about 0.27 km³)?
items.answer: VEI 6; 85.2 / 0.27 = 316 times the volume of Eyjafjallajökull 2010
items.markingKey: A1 VEI 6 (85.2 km³ lies between 10 and 100 km³). A1 ratio 316.

items.stem: Distinguish between vulnerability and exposure.
items.answer: Exposure is the presence of people and assets in a hazard zone; vulnerability is their susceptibility to harm, which depends on factors such as building quality, wealth and preparedness.
items.markingKey: Exposure is the presence of people and assets in a hazard zone; vulnerability is their susceptibility to harm, which depends on factors such as building quality, wealth and preparedness. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Hong Kong's slope safety programme as an example, explain management of landslide risk.
items.answer: Since 1977 the Geotechnical Engineering Office has upgraded thousands of man-made slopes, sharply reducing landslide deaths. Engineering, mapping and warnings can reduce risk on steep urban slopes.
items.markingKey: Context (Since 1977 the Geotechnical Engineering Office has upgraded thousands of man-made slopes, sharply reducing landslide deaths.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Engineering, mapping and warnings can reduce risk on steep urban slopes. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to management of landslide risk.

items.stem: Examine the view that hazard magnitude is more important than frequency in determining hazard risk.
items.answer: Both matter: rare high-magnitude events dominate losses, but frequency shapes preparedness and long-term costs.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: high-magnitude events cause most deaths and losses (Tōhoku, Sumatra); they exceed the capacity of defences. Against / limitations: frequent small events cause cumulative damage and losses; frequency affects preparedness and perception. A supported conclusion might be: Both matter: rare high-magnitude events dominate losses, but frequency shapes preparedness and long-term costs. items.stem: Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana together produce about what share of world cocoa?
items.answer: About 60%
items.markingKey: About 60%. Most of the value is added by chocolate companies in Europe and the USA.

items.stem: According to the UN, each additional year of secondary schooling for girls can raise their future earnings by about:
items.markingKey: 10-20%. Education also lowers fertility and child mortality.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the world has not "shrunk" equally for all places.
items.answer: Connections are concentrated between global cities and well-connected regions; remote, poor and landlocked places have fewer flights, slower internet and higher costs, so relative distance remains large (the digital divide). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Connections are concentrated between global cities and well-connected regions; remote, poor and landlocked places have fewer flights, slower internet and higher costs, so relative distance remains large (the digital divide). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between state actors and non-state actors.
items.answer: State actors are governments and their agencies (militaries, intelligence services); non-state actors include terrorist groups, hackers, TNCs and NGOs.
items.markingKey: State actors are governments and their agencies (militaries, intelligence services); non-state actors include terrorist groups, hackers, TNCs and NGOs. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Labour migration brings more benefits to source countries than costs." To what extent do you agree with this statement? In your answer, consider the perspectives of different places and scales.
items.answer: Benefits are significant, but losses of skilled workers can harm services in small source countries.

items.stem: Households in a ward in Bristol by tenure: owner-occupied 357, privately rented 205, social housing 489. A student will interview 60 households using stratified sampling. Calculate how many of each tenure type should be interviewed, and give one advantage of stratified sampling here.

items.answer: Description states what the data show (patterns, trends, values); analysis explains why, using geographical theory, statistical tests and links to the fieldwork question.

items.answer: A hazard produced directly by the geophysical event, such as ground shaking, lava flows or pyroclastic flows

items.answer: downtown Tokyo: 48.0; a hillside favela in Rio de Janeiro: 21.0; greater risk: downtown Tokyo

items.stem: Explain how heavy rainfall can trigger landslides.
items.answer: Water infiltrates and raises pore-water pressure, reducing friction and cohesion (shear strength), while adding weight that increases shear stress; when stress exceeds strength the slope fails.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Water infiltrates and raises pore-water pressure, reducing friction and cohesion (shear strength), while adding weight that increases shear stress; when stress exceeds strength the slope fails. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake, Italy, explain how it illustrates the limits of earthquake prediction.
items.answer: A Mw 6.3 earthquake killed 309 people after experts were accused of giving false reassurance. Foreshocks did not allow scientists to predict the main shock reliably.
items.markingKey: Context (A Mw 6.3 earthquake killed 309 people after experts were accused of giving false reassurance.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Foreshocks did not allow scientists to predict the main shock reliably. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the limits of earthquake prediction.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that earthquake magnitude is the most important factor in determining earthquake impacts?
items.answer: Magnitude sets the potential, but vulnerability and local conditions largely determine impacts.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: higher magnitude releases more energy and shakes larger areas; great earthquakes can trigger tsunamis (Tōhoku 2011). Against / limitations: Haiti 2010 (Mw 7.0) killed far more than Chile 2010 (Mw 8.8); depth, distance, geology, buildings and preparedness determine impacts. A supported conclusion might be: Magnitude sets the potential, but vulnerability and local conditions largely determine impacts. items.answer: The Montreal Protocol has binding phase-out schedules for a few specific chemicals and near-universal compliance; the Paris Agreement relies on voluntary national pledges covering all greenhouse gases from the whole economy.

items.stem: A fieldwork survey recorded the shape (Powers' categories) of 80 pebbles sampled on a river bar in Snowdonia: angular 14, sub-angular 16, sub-rounded 23, rounded 27. items.stem: Approximate data for Chile: life expectancy 79.5 years; expected years of schooling 16.8; mean years of schooling 11.1; GNI per capita US$25,000 (PPP). Using the UNDP method - life expectancy index = (LE − 20)/65; education index = (MYS/15 + EYS/18)/2, with EYS capped at 18; income index = (ln GNI − ln 100)/(ln 75,000 − ln 100); HDI = geometric mean of the three indices - calculate the HDI and its category. items.answer: LEI 0.915; EI 0.837; II 0.834; HDI = (0.915 × 0.837 × 0.834)^(1/3) = 0.861 (very high human development); weakest dimension: income.

items.stem: At a road cutting in Kerala, the shear strength of the regolith is 102 kPa and the shear stress acting down the slope is 76 kPa. Calculate the factor of safety (strength ÷ stress). Intense rainfall then raises pore-water pressure, reducing shear strength by 15%. Calculate the new factor of safety and state whether the slope is likely to fail.
items.answer: FS = 102/76 = 1.34; after rain FS = 86.7/76 = 1.14; stable but marginal (FS ≥ 1)
items.markingKey: A1 FS 1.34; M1 strength reduced by 15%; A1 FS 1.14; R1 FS < 1 means failure.
